content.comment_body: Hello everyone, I'm new to [product_name] and, after struggling and relying heavily on forum support, I've managed to create a few programs. My concern is how to keep a growing block diagram organized. Although my program functions well, its structure lacks clarity. Does anyone have suggestions for maintaining neat, organized diagrams as your projects expand? Any advice would be much appreciated.

To adjust your diagram layout, click the 'Page Layout' icon in the editor's menu bar. A pop-up will let you set the number of vertical and horizontal pages for your diagram. See the video attachment for reference.

Thank you for your response. I already use the page layout function and have it set to 2 wide by 3 high. My real question is more about general program organization strategies. Regardless of what the program does, is there a recommended way to format or lay out the diagrams for better clarity?

There's no universal method for organizing diagrams; it often depends on individual preferences. However, there are some best practices to consider: - Avoid overlapping connection lines between blocks. - Keep sufficient space between blocks to maintain readability. - Use block comments to clarify the function of individual blocks when necessary. - Provide additional documentation for groups of blocks that work together.

From my experience: 1. The line cut tool can be quite useful. 2. You can use text to create lines if you need them visually. 3. Adjust your page size based on your printer settings. I've attached a formatting concept for reference, but only a portion due to intellectual property restrictions. I cannot share the full unedited program.

After organizing my program for better structure and flow, I've encountered a new issue—my [article_no] BM is out of layout memory with a usage of 33032 where the max is 30000. Input 1 now activates 37 other points, creating significant complexity and clutter, so I used the 'Separate' command to tidy things up. That's the only adjustment made. Is there a way to optimize the layout to use less memory, or increase the available layout memory? Discussions in forums suggest this doesn't impact the actual program operation. Here are my current resource stats: Function Blocks 169/400; Digital Inputs 9/24; Digital Outputs 12/20; Flags 15/64; Analog Inputs 0/8; Text Boxes 0/50; Text Contents 0/50; Analog Outputs 2/8; Program Memory 2492/8500; Block Names 21/100; Analog Flags 8/64; Cursor Keys 0/4; Shift Registers 0/4; Shift Register Bits 0/32; Open Connectors 7/64; [product_name] TD Function Keys 0/4; Network Inputs 12/64; Network Analog Inputs 4/32; UDF Types 0/16; UDF Instances 0/64; Data Log 0/1; Network Outputs 5/64; Network Analog Outputs 0/16; Analog Filters 0/8; Layout Memory 33032/30000. Maximum nesting depth: I1-B001-B002-B003 INTERVAL-B004-B005 RANDOM-B006-B007 WAKE UP-B045-B046-B008-B055-Q1.

Layout memory is fixed and cannot be expanded. It simply holds the positions of blocks and paths of connections in the diagram. Full layout memory won't impact program functionality. The issue only arises when you reload the program from the device to your PC—blocks may be arranged chaotically, and lines may overlap, making the diagram harder to read.

Hi [user_name], Personally, I use the line cut tool sparingly and prefer to cluster related blocks together for clarity, keeping descriptive text minimal. Full program descriptions are best stored in the comments section under 'Properties'. For repeatable or complex sections I want to reuse later, I create UDFs—developing and documenting them separately so I can easily use and specify parameters in future projects. Managing UDFs requires organization, and I maintain a dedicated demo program for detailed UDF descriptions. I add comment descriptions as needed and assign meaningful text colors (e.g., red for important info). The goal is to make the project understandable to anyone, even years later, while avoiding excessive documentation.

Hi [user_name], thank you for your insights. Thanks to advice from the forums, I've organized my program to be much clearer and easier to follow. This particular project isn't used in a real application—it's mainly for learning and as a hobby.
Even for hobby projects, it's important to maintain clarity and organization. Regards, [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: The main challenge discussed is maintaining organized and structured block diagrams in [product_name] software as projects grow more complex. While tools for layout and documentation exist, organizing diagrams may lead to layout memory limitations, resulting in visual disarray when reloading programs, although this does not impact core functionality. Participants are seeking better layout management strategies, effective documentation, and ways to optimize memory usage for long-term usability and clarity.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect to be able to effectively organize large, complex block diagrams within [product_name] without running into layout memory limits, and to maintain a clear, readable flow in their diagrams as project complexity increases.
